videos.script:
Two projects on one machine. {{comment}} One of them was written three years ago and needs an old version of a library; the other was started this morning and needs the new one. Both are `import requests`, and there is one Python.

{{answer}} The answer is an environment per project. A directory, inside the project, holding its own copy of every library it uses — so the two never meet, and neither of them is the machine's Python.

{{system}} That last part is not a preference. The interpreter at `/usr/bin/python3` belongs to the operating system, and things you did not write import from it. Installing into it is editing somebody else's dependency, and on a modern distribution it now refuses: `error: externally-managed-environment`.

{{venv}} `python -m venv .venv` makes one. It is a directory with a `bin`, a `lib` and a small configuration file, and `activate` puts its `bin` at the front of your `PATH` so that `python` means that one.

{{gitignore}} It is **never committed**. It holds compiled artefacts for one operating system and one processor, and it is rebuilt from a text file in five seconds.

{{pip}} `pip` installs into whichever environment is active — which is where a whole category of confusion comes from, so this lesson writes `python -m pip` throughout. It is the same program, reached in a way that cannot be pointing somewhere else.

{{versions}} Then the version specifiers, which look obvious and are not. `~=2.31.0` and `~=2.31` are different requests, and in a fresh environment this afternoon they resolved to different versions.

{{freeze}} And `pip freeze`, which everybody uses to write `requirements.txt` and which is **not a requirements file**. It is a list of everything installed, direct and transitive, flattened into one list where nothing says which of them you actually asked for.

The same `import requests`, twice, on this machine. {{comment}} Two directories, two environments, two versions.

{{first}} `python -m venv .venv` in the first project, activate it, `python -m pip install requests==2.31.0`. Then `python -c "import requests; print(requests.__version__)"` says **2.31.0**, and `requests.__file__` is inside that project's directory.

{{second}} The second project, in a directory beside it. Its own `venv`, `requests==2.26.0`. Same command, and it says **2.26.0**.

{{nothing}} Nothing was configured to make that work. `activate` put one `bin` at the front of the `PATH`, `sys.prefix` moved, and the import found the first `requests` on `sys.path` — which is now that environment's `site-packages` and nothing else.

{{path}} Worth looking at that path, because it explains the other half of this lesson. `sys.path` for the first project is five entries: the empty string, two standard-library directories, the dynamic-load directory, and **one** `site-packages`. The machine's libraries are not on it at all.

{{shadow}} The empty string is the current directory, and it is **first**. A file called `json.py` in the project directory is what `import json` finds, ahead of the standard library — `json.__file__` points at your file and the error you get is about your own code, three imports away from where you are looking.

{{freeze}} One last thing from the first environment. `pip freeze` prints five lines: `requests` and four libraries I never asked for. `requirements.txt` should carry one of those five, and the difference between those two lists is the subject of the two sections before this.

One environment per project, and never the system interpreter.

{{make}} `python -m venv .venv` on the first day, before the first install. Doing it later means unpicking what went into the machine's Python in the meantime, which nobody does.

{{ignore}} `.venv/` in `.gitignore`, and the file that reproduces it committed instead. The directory is a build artefact for one machine; the text file is the fact.

{{pip}} `python -m pip`, not `pip`. The second one is a script with a path baked into it, and when it is the wrong one nothing says so — the install succeeds, into somewhere else.

{{freeze}} `pip freeze` is a snapshot, not a declaration. Write what you asked for into `requirements.txt`, by hand, with the version you tested against; let a lock file carry the rest.

{{pin}} And pin the transitive half somewhere, or an install that worked yesterday fails today because a library you have never heard of released a new version inside a range you did not choose.

{{next}} All of which the next lesson replaces with one file and one tool, and it is still worth knowing — because the repository you join on Monday is on `requirements.txt` and somebody has to read it.
